title: The mistakes notebook: one page per error
description: Not a diary of shame — a field guide to your own patterns. Each mistake gets one page: what happened, what it cost, and the one-line cue that will catch it next time. Reviewed monthly, it quietly stops history repeating.

body.heading: The one-page rule
paragraphs: Keep a cheap notebook for mistakes only. When something goes wrong that you could repeat — a missed deadline, a mis-sent message, a burnt dinner, a lost argument you should have won kindly — give it one page and three headings: What happened (facts only, no adjectives about yourself). What it cost (time, money, trust, sleep). The cue (one short sentence your future self can act on: 'Check the attachment before the apology.').
One page is the whole discipline. A mistake that needs three pages of analysis is usually being punished, not studied — and punishment teaches avoidance, not skill. Facts, cost, cue, close the book.

body.heading: The monthly harvest
paragraphs: Once a month, read the notebook cover to cover with a pen in hand. You are hunting for repeats: the same cue appearing three times is not three mistakes, it is one system asking to be redesigned. Move that cue somewhere it cannot be skipped — a checklist, a phone reminder, a note on the door.

Expect the notebook to thin out over time in the best way: whole categories of error retire as their cues become habits. The mistakes that remain will be new ones, which is what progress actually looks like from the inside.

takeaway: Give each repeatable mistake one page — facts, cost, and a one-line cue — then harvest the repeats monthly and turn the commonest cue into a system.
materials: A cheap notebook kept only for mistakes
A pen that lives with the notebook
Ten quiet minutes after a mistake, and thirty minutes once a month for the review
supervision: No supervision is required; this is a private reflective activity for adults and older children.
safetyNotes: Keep the notebook private and store it somewhere others will not read it — honesty on the page depends on it staying yours alone.
Write facts, not verdicts about your character; if reviewing mistakes leaves you distressed rather than clearer, close the book and return another day.
